title: Does your 2 November ruling, that "compile" means the printed listing, still stand now that the fact behind it is corrected?
today: The 1960 manual prints a payroll program. We key it exactly as printed, and it draws 55 error messages. Our compiler prints the full listing, and a test checks it byte for byte. Then code generation stops and punches no object deck, the cards that hold the machine program. It stops at a read of a record that no file supplies, and it has a second refusal for writing a record into a file that is not one of its output files. The corrected version of the program compiles to a 68-card object deck.
why_now: On 2 November you ruled that "compile", in your 14 September rule, means the listing. The pitch told you the 1962 compiler refused to punch a deck for this program. That was wrong: it punched a deck and did not run it. You decided on a false fact, so you should confirm. No code waits on the answer.
if_nothing: Your 2 November ruling stands as recorded. Pull request 182, already merged, records the listing reading, and the compiler keeps refusing the deck at those spots.

options.label: Yes, it stands
options.what_changes: Nothing changes. We print the full listing and refuse the object deck where no source shows the code. The design record already says that the 1962 compiler punched the deck and did not run it.
options.cost_risk: No cost. A reader could ask why we stop where 1962 went on. The record answers that question.
options.reverse: Easy. A later decision can still build the deck code.

options.label: No: punch the object deck as 1962 did
options.what_changes: The generator would emit code for a read of a record with no input file, a write to a file that is not an output file, and the 26 references to undefined names. It would then punch a deck.
options.cost_risk: No manual and no surviving listing shows that code, so we invent all of it. The 1962 system did not run this deck, so nothing can check it. Several days of design work with no oracle.
options.reverse: Hard. Invented code enters the generator and the tests, and taking it out later is a second change.

recommendation: Keep the ruling. The listing is still the only reading that needs no invented code. No source shows what the 1962 deck held, so any code we wrote for these spots could not be checked. The corrected fact changes the story, not the cost.
prototype: Pull request 182, merged, records the listing reading in the acceptance design record and relabels the two refusals in code comments only. It also corrects the wrong fact about the deck. No compiler behaviour changed.

scenes.caption: From our listing of the 1960 program as printed. The 4 is the severity.
scenes.say: The program reads a record that no file supplies, and writes a record to no output file. The listing flags both. Our generator refuses to invent code for these spots, so it stops.

scenes.heading: The fact the pitch got wrong
bullets: The pitch said the 1962 compiler refused to punch a deck. It did not.
1962 manual, 02.01.01: "If the severity code is 5, a deck will not be produced."
1962 manual, 90.04.02: any code above 1 stops the run straight after compiling
Our highest code here is 4, so 1962 punched the deck and did not run it
scenes.say: The pitch said the 1962 compiler refused the deck. Wrong. It withheld a deck only at severity five. Our worst code here is four. So 1962 punched a deck, but did not run it.
